title: Historical fluxes and enrichment factors of trace elements in Lake Erie sediments
description: Publication date: Available online 1 June 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Mahsa Tashakor, Anthony Chappaz
abstract: The Lake Erie watershed, the most densely populated of the Laurentian Great Lakes, has experienced significant trace element (TE) contamination over the past two centuries due to industrialization, agriculture, and urbanization. This study examines the sedimentary profiles of cadmium, chromium, copper, antimony, tungsten and zinc in a sediment core from the Central Basin of Lake Erie to reconstruct historical fluxes and enrichment factors for all these TEs in relation to anthropogenic impacts on the lake's watershed over the last century. Using 210Pb geochronology and 137Cs activity, sediment mass accumulation rates were determined, revealing that the Central Basin experienced the highest sediment loading among the Great Lakes during the second half of the 20th century. This coincides with increased TE inputs probably driven by industrial activities, fossil fuel combustion, and land-use changes. We identified four distinct periods of TE fluxes: (1) pre-1900, with minimal anthropogenic influence; (2) early to mid-1900s, characterized by rapid industrialization and a sharp rise in TE concentrations; (3) 1950s to 1990, marked by ongoing industrial and agricultural contamination; and (4) 1990–2014, when regulatory efforts contributed to a substantial decline in TE levels. Yet the levels of Sn and W in the top sediments remain concerning. Industrial processes were the primary source of TE contamination, and we present new evidence linking W contamination to historical tungsten production in the region. These findings underscore the lasting environmental impact of human activities on Lake Erie’s sediments and emphasize the need for continued and improved monitoring and mitigation.

title: Preferential authigenic clay precipitation on microbial mats in alkaline lakes of the Cariboo Plateau, British Columbia, Canada
description: Publication date: Available online 1 June 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Maria L. Arizaleta, Maija J. Raudsepp, Nina Zeyen, Janice P.L. Kenney, Cody Lazowski, Daniel S. Alessi, Kurt O. Konhauser, Sasha Wilson
abstract: Alkaline lakes commonly precipitate authigenic Mg-phyllosilicates, yet the controls on formation of these clay minerals remain poorly understood. This study examines the geochemical and microbial controls on precipitation of Mg-rich clays and carbonates in four alkaline lakes of the Cariboo Plateau located in British Columbia, Canada. Mineralogical analyses reveal that lake sediments and microbial mats contain abundant stevensite [(Na2y ·nH2O) (Mg3–y □ y )Si4O10(OH)2], a Mg-clay phase typically associated with high-alkalinity, closed-basin systems. Mg-carbonates are also present, magnesite (MgCO3) and very high Mg-calcite [also known as disordered dolomite, (Ca0.5Mg0.5CO3)]. Despite extremely low aqueous Mg and Si concentrations, we observe that Mg-clay precipitation is favoured over Mg-carbonates within microbial mats compared to sediment from the same lake. Our findings suggest that microbial processes, including cyanobacterial activity and diatom frustule dissolution, play a key role in facilitating Mg-clay formation by influencing local geochemical conditions and providing nucleation sites. These findings highlight the importance of considering microbial activity when using lacustrine sediments as paleoenvironmental proxies, as they can significantly impact the mineralogical composition of the sediment associated with the microbial mat.

title: The Role of Ionic Strength in Regulating the Sorption Mechanism of Zn on Palygorskite: From Outer-Sphere Complexes to Polynuclear Species
description: Publication date: Available online 1 June 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Xinxin Mo, Wanru Ouyang, Qi Long, Wei Li, Xueyuan Gu, Yoshio Takahashi, Jianbo Shi
abstract: Zinc (Zn) contamination poses significant risks to soil and water quality, necessitating effective remediation strategies. Palygorskite, a fibrous clay mineral, shows strong potential as an adsorbent, but the molecular-scale mechanisms governing Zn sorption, particularly the role of ionic strength, remain unclear. Here, by integrating batch sorption experiments, surface complexation modeling (SCM), and Zn K-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectroscopy, this study suggests that ionic strength may act as a key factor influencing Zn(II) sorption mechanisms on palygorskite across varying pH (4.0-7.5) and ionic strength (0.001-0.1 M NaNO3). Macroscopic data revealed that ionic strength strongly suppressed Zn uptake at low pH via competition for permanent-charge sites, but became negligible under alkaline conditions, consistent with SCM quantification of outer-sphere (OS) complexes on basal sites and inner-sphere (IS) complexes on edge sites. XAFS analysis at both 80 and 800 μM Zn provides direct molecular-scale evidence for a pivotal mechanistic shift: at pH 7.5, elevated ionic strength (0.1 M) promoted the formation of polynuclear IS complexes even at a relatively low concentration (80 μM), acting as precursors to surface precipitation. This contrasts with the mononuclear species dominant at low ionic strength despite comparable total uptake, and is further corroborated by the formation of polynuclear complexes at higher Zn concentration (800 μM) even under low ionic strength. We propose that elevated ionic strength may compress the electrical double layer and compete for basal sites, thereby promoting Zn redistribution to reactive edge sites where increased local coverage favors nucleation. This work redefines ionic strength from a competitive background parameter to an active regulator of adsorption-to-nucleation transitions on clay minerals, providing a predictive framework for Zn sequestration in fluctuating ionic environments and guiding the design of palygorskite-based remediation strategies.

title: Stable versus transient sulfate–methane transition zone dynamics recorded by coexisting concretion types: Petrographic and in situ sulfur isotope evidence from Lower Silurian shale
description: Publication date: Available online 1 June 2026 Source: Chemical Geology Author(s): Shichao Ji, Chao Liang, Jing Wu, Yingchang Cao, Keyu Liu, Fang Hao, Qing Tang
abstract: Authigenic concretions in marine mudstones preserve spatially resolved pore-water records during early diagenesis, yet whether mineralogically distinct concretion types differentially archive stable versus shifting sulfate–methane transition zone (SMTZ) conditions remains unresolved. This study combines petrography with in situ δ34S analyses at concretion-scale zone mapping and grain-scale core-to-rim profiling to investigate pyrite concretions and quartz–calcite concretions from the Lower Silurian Longmaxi Formation, South China. Pyrite concretions display mineralogically uniform interiors and a modest concretion-scale δ34Spyr gradient, with mean values of ~11.5‰ at the margin and ~ 7.8‰ at the center. Where multiple spots per grain are available, intra-grain profiles show no coherent core-to-rim trend, although spot coverage is limited. These features are consistent with relatively rapid pervasive mineralization within a narrow diagenetic interval. Their intermediate δ34Spyr values indicate mixing between 34S-depleted OSR-related reduced sulfur and a relatively 34S-enriched SMTZ-associated reduced‑sulfur component. Quartz–calcite concretions preserve a contrasting multi-stage record. An inverted concretion-scale δ34Spyr pattern, with relatively 34S-depleted margin pyrite and more 34S-enriched center pyrite, together with repeated grain-scale core-to-rim 34S enrichment, records sequential pyrite formation during progressive burial from the sulfate reduction zone into the SMTZ. Pseudomorphic replacement of diagenetic barite by quartz and calcite provides independent mineralogical evidence for subsequent burial into sulfate-depleted conditions within or below the SMTZ. The outermost overgrowth zone, characterized by acicular barite pseudomorphs, 34S-enriched pyrite, and grain-scale core-to-rim δ34S increases, records transient paleo-SMTZ descent and renewed SMTZ influence during continued burial. This transient SMTZ deepening is consistent with reduced methane substrate supply during Aeronian forced regression, which may have been linked to Kwangsian Orogeny-related regional sedimentological reorganization, although this tectonic linkage remains inferential. These results demonstrate that mineralogically distinct concretions preserve complementary, stage-specific records of paleo-SMTZ dynamics and provide new constraints on early diagenetic sulfur cycling in ancient marine successions.

title: Long-term and interannual variability of African terrestrial water storage revealed by GRACE/GRACE-FO and models
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Guodong Xu, Jianli Chen, Yufeng Nie, Shuo Zheng, Jing Li
abstract: Climate change is intensifying the hydrologic cycle, and terrestrial water storage (TWS) provides an integrated indicator of these shifts. In this study, we analyzed long-term and interannual TWS variations across Africa over April 2002-December 2024 using GRACE/GRACE Follow-On (GRACE/-FO) satellite gravimetry, together with land surface models (LSMs) and satellite altimetry derived lake storage. GRACE/-FO revealed a continental TWS increase of 96.1 ± 13.4 Gt yr−1 (2σ), with an acceleration of 11.6 ± 3.83 Gt yr−2. Basin-scale attribution exhibited that large lakes/reservoirs storage increases largely contributed to the observed TWS gains, whereas model predicted soil moisture showed a general declining trend, likely indicating the limitations of LSMs in this region. The long-term TWS increase was further quantitatively supported by a rising water balance. Interannual variability was structured by large-scale climate modes: El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) paced continental and tripole-like responses, respectively, as identified by empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis. Our results elucidated new observational constraints on the drivers of African TWS dynamics and their responses to a changing climate.

title: Precision mapping of evapotranspiration in arid basins: Spatiotemporal optimization and sensitivity to extreme climate conditions based on multi-mechanism model fusion
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Xiang Li, Jinlong Shi, Jianli Ding, Tongren Xu, Lisheng Song, Jinjie Wang, Ziwei Xu, Dongxing Wu, Xinlei He, Yuan Zhang, Zijie Pang, Feihu Xue, Ziyan Xu
abstract: Conventional ground-based ET measurements are inadequate for large-scale areas, while remote sensing models exhibit inconsistent accuracy over heterogeneous surfaces due to variations in physical mechanisms and parameterization schemes. This study, based on remote sensing data from 2012 to 2016, utilized the Surface Energy Balance Algorithm for Land (SEBAL), Surface Energy Balance System (SEBS), Penman-Monteith (PM) and Priestley-Taylor (PT) models to estimate evapotranspiration (ET) in the Heihe River Basin. After the multi-model resultswerefused and optimized using Triple Collocation (TC) and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) methods, the model accuracywassystematically evaluated across various spatial (site and basin) and temporal scales, as well as across diverse land cover types, with a further sensitivity analysis conducted under extreme heat conditions. The results showed that, the SEBAL achieved the highest accuracy (R = 0.76, RMSE = 1.18 mm/day), followed by PM (R = 0.74, RMSE = 1.28 mm/day) and SEBS (R = 0.72, RMSE = 1.34 mm/day), and the PT model had the lowest accuracy (R = 0.65, RMSE = 1.47 mm/day); Among the single models, SEBAL showed slightly higher accuracy, but each exhibited biases under specific land cover types or climatic conditions. To overcome this limitation, fusion models (TC_PET and MLE_PET) were developed, leveraging the strengths of individual models to achieve superior overall accuracy, the fusion models demonstrated significantly higher accuracy (R ≥ 0.79, RMSE < 0.9 mm/day) than single models. Spatially, ET exhibited a decreasing trend from upstream to downstream regions, with the highest values in the upper reaches and the lowest in the lower reaches. Under extreme high-temperature conditions, single-model accuracy significantly declined. Fusion models can effectively reduce such errors and uncertainties, and they achieve the most significant improvement in accuracy over single models in complex surface scenarios such as croplands and grasslands. The proposed fusion framework substantially enhances the reliability and robustness of ET estimation in complex environments, providing theoretical and technical support for water resource management and ecological conservation in arid/semi-arid regions.

title: Performance-based assessment of tropical cyclone parametric precipitation models for flood simulation applications
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Orlando M. Viloria-Marimón, Felix L. Santiago-Collazo, Matthew V. Bilskie, Avantika Gori, Thomas L. Mote
abstract: Tropical cyclone (TC) rainfall is one of the primary drivers of flooding in coastal watersheds; therefore, accurate rainfall estimation is essential for reliable hydrologic and hydraulic (H&H) modeling. In TC-prone regions like the Caribbean Islands, which are also topographically complex, the wide range of models available for estimating TC rainfall presents a challenge in identifying the most suitable Parametric Precipitation Models (PPMs) for flood modeling applications. Thus, this study proposes a dual-component framework for benchmarking PPM-derived rainfall: (i) a rainfall-level comparison of PPMs and (ii) a performance-based assessment of the rainfall fields produced by PPMs for flood simulations applications. The proposed framework was applied to a watershed in Puerto Rico and tested under three historical hurricanes using five PPMs and Stage IV radar-based rainfall as a benchmark. The rainfall-level analysis assessed precipitation accumulation distribution, patterns, and cumulative totals, while the performance-based assessment examined the impacts on riverine flow timing, peak discharge, and overland flood levels in the selected watershed. Results show that the Parametric Hurricane Rainfall Model (PHRaM) and its shear-excluded variant performed most consistently across all metrics. However, PPM-derived rainfall fields are unreliable for real-time forecasting in their current state. Importantly, simulated peak flows were more affected by the rainfall uncertainty than flood extents. Thus, this study highlights the need to select an appropriate tool for assessing flood risk, particularly in steep, complex terrain. Although PPMs are efficient in data-scarce regions, their inherent structural limitations must be carefully evaluated to ensure reliable flood hazard predictions.

title: A novel fusion framework for generating 30 m daily seamless soil moisture with reliable performance
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yangxiaoyue Liu, Ying Xin, Yuan Tian
abstract: High-resolution (30 m) daily soil moisture (SM) dataset is critical for precision agriculture, drought monitoring, and water resource management. However, such dataset remains challenging to obtain due to the limited spatial and temporal resolutions in existing satellite products. To address this issue, this study proposes a novel two-step deep learning framework to produce a high-resolution (30 m) daily seamless SM with reliable accuracy, leveraging strengths from open-access remotely sensed products, terrain, and soil property datasets. The framework is independent from in-situ measurements. First, a convolutional neural network-based super-resolution model (MSRNet) downscales 500 m MODIS spectral bands (8 bands including visible, near-infrared, and thermal infrared) to 30 m resolution using Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel (HLS) data of the corresponding 8 bands. Second, a SM simulation network (SMSNet) learns the relationship between SM and 16 explanatory variables, including the downscaled MODIS bands, terrain features, soil properties, and 1 km SMAP/Sentinel SM at an intermediate resolution of 125 m. Third, the trained SMSNet is applied to 30 m inputs to generate seamless daily high-resolution SM estimations. Validated against in-situ measurements in Naqu (central Tibet Plateau) with significance test (p < 0.01), the 30 m SM achieves significant accuracy improvements over the original SMAP/Sentinel product, with increased correlation (R = 0.70 vs. 0.68) and reduced errors (RMSE = 0.09 m3/m3 vs. 0.12 m3/m3, ubRMSE = 0.07 m3/m3 vs. 0.10 m3/m3). Moreover, the cross-regional validation is conducted at the Maqu (northeast Tibet Plateau) for generalizability and transferability test of the established SMSNet, and achieves reasonable performances. This research provides a feasible solution for large spatial–temporal scale improvement of SM simulation through the combination of MSRNet and SMSNet, enabling field-scale SM applications, as demonstrated in the Tibetan Plateau region, without reliance on ground-based networks.

title: Temporal inductive biases in hourly flood forecasting: a comparative analysis of recurrent, attention-based, and state-space neural networks
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Binlan Zhang, Chaojun Ouyang, Qingsong Xu, Yanlin Liu, Zili Wang, Quan Tang
abstract: Daily-resolution flood forecasts often encounter difficulties in capturing rapid runoff fluctuations over short time periods. To address this limitation, moving to hourly-scale modeling is essential, yet identifying which deep learning architectures possess the optimal temporal inductive biases for such high-frequency dynamics remains an open challenge. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive comparative analysis of recurrent, attention-based, and state-space neural networks, benchmarked against simple layered structures on discharge-assisted forecasting tasks across 516 CAMELS catchments. The results indicate that the Patch Transformer achieves the best predictive performance. This suggests that patch-based processing acts as a superior inductive bias by smoothing high-frequency noise and extracting local temporal semantics, which effectively captures long-term routing and hydrological dependencies better than point-wise attention. While the traditional LSTM maintains robust performance, the Mamba model demonstrates a promising balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, through an interpretability analysis combining attention weights with Integrated Gradients (IG), we reveal that attention models successfully capture physical hydrological patterns, such as time-lagged responses and the dominance of dynamic meteorological drivers over static attributes. This work offers theoretical insights into how architectural choices determine short-term forecasting capability under diverse hydro-climatic regimes.

title: Streamflow seasonality responds to changes in snowfall fraction in the Upper Indus Basin
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yixuan Wang, Yan-Jun Shen, Xiaolong Zhang, Muhammad Zaman, Muhammad Imran Khan
abstract: Variations in snowfall fraction (SF) drive streamflow timing shifts globally, yet basin-specific patterns and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This is particularly critical for the climate-vulnerable, snow-dependent Upper Indus Basin (UIB) where significant sub-basin differences in SF influence streamflow seasonality. Here, we investigate the impacts of variations in SF on streamflow seasonality in the UIB across various sub-basins from 1971 to 2017 using streamflow center time (QCT) and concentration index (QCI), with sensitivity indices quantifying precipitation timing (PCT) versus snowmelt onset timing (MOD) controls. We find that the Karakoram sub-basins (Shyok, Hunza, and Shigar) exhibited the highest SF (0.82–0.88) in the UIB; despite an overall declining trend basin-wide, 64% of the area showed increasing SF trends, with significant rises in high-altitude zones. Higher SF correlates with later (increased QCT) and more concentrated (higher QCI) streamflow, especially in Karakoram basins. Crucially, we identify an SF threshold of 0.8 that triggers a regime shift where MOD replaces PCT as the primary driver of runoff timing. This threshold provides a mechanistic explanation for the Karakoram’s distinctive “accumulation-concentration-lag” phenomenon, revealing that its high-altitude snowpack acts as a physical buffer that stabilizes seasonal streamflow and delays the hydrological response to early-season warming.

title: Hydro-mechanical coupling between pore pressure and crustal deformation following earthquakes: insights from groundwater tidal response and InSAR analysis
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Luoyao Xiong, Guanru He, Zheming Shi, Guangcai Wang, Zhiyu Qi, Peng Ye, Guoying Li
abstract: Hydro-mechanical coupling in the shallow crust affects a suite of geological processes such as tectonism, seismicity, deposition and erosion dynamics. However, direct field observations that illustrate the coupling between the pore pressure and crustal deformation remain scarce. Here, we combine Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) and groundwater tidal response analysis to quantify the co-seismic and post-seismic impacts of the 2022 Luding (Ms 6.8) and Menyuan (Ms 6.9) earthquakes on crustal permeability, vertical displacement patterns, and groundwater-level fluctuations. The results show that the temporal trend of crustal permeability shifts from progressive enhancement to gradual attenuation following earthquake, together with a transition from surface uplift to subsidence in wells proximal to the active fault and the epicenter. Furthermore, the observed co-seismic groundwater-level steps are generally consistent with the modeled static strain field, showing rises in compressional zones and declines in extensional zones for most wells (e.g., MY, SMC20, SMC49), although exceptions exist (e.g., well ZS). The cross-correlation analyzes revealed strengthened correlations between permeability evolution and vertical displacement during the post-seismic phase compared to pre-seismic phase, indicating substantial reorganization of subsurface fault architectures and fluid pathways induced by seismic strain. Our results from five monitoring wells provide site-specific observations of the transient relationships between subsurface fluid dynamics and surface deformation during hydro-mechanical perturbations in active tectonic regions.

title: How does the roots architecture affect the runoff –infiltration –erosion processes under varying rainfall events?
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Lin Zhang, Yutong Li, Bingchen Wu, Shi Qi
abstract: Plant roots play a critical role in regulating surface–belowground hydrological processes, yet the mechanisms by which root regulates runoff, infiltration and erosion under different rainfall events remain insufficiently understood. In this study, root–soil composites of Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis) with three stand densities, including high-density (S1: 2400 plants ha–1), medium-density (S2: 2000 plants ha–1), and low-density (S3: 1600 plants ha–1), were investigated. Controlled rainfall simulations representing low (20 mm h–1), moderate (30 mm h–1), and high (40 mm h–1) rainfall intensities were applied to quantify the dynamic movement processes of surface runoff, subsurface flow, vertical infiltration and surface sediment were collected and quantified using a custom-designed soil water movement monitoring device. Root architecture and soil pore structure were quantified using CT scanning and pore network modelling. Structural equation modelling was further applied to elucidate root–pore–hydrology linkages. Results indicate that (1) under low to moderate rainfall (20–30 mm h–1), subsurface flow was the dominant hydrological component, accounting for 49.87%–88.70% in S1, 50.57%–89.20% in S2, and 41.60%–81.60% in S3 of the total runoff and infiltration amount. In contrast, under high-intensity rainfall (40 mm h–1), surface runoff became dominant, contributing 72.6%–75.0% across all densities, surface runoff rates ranged from 0.052–0.486 L min–1 m–2 across treatments. (2) Relative to S3, under 20–30 mm h–1, surface runoff and sediment yield in S1 and S2 were 11%–32% and 31%–62% lower, respectively, while subsurface flow in the 10–20 cm and 20–40 cm layers increased by 48.31%–54.68% and 27.76%–30.59%, respectively. However, under 40 mm h–1, no significant density effects were detected for runoff partitioning or sediment yield (P＞0.05). (3) Root effects were mainly indirect and mediated by pore structural changes: the total effects of throat radius, connected porosity, and throat length on surface runoff were − 0.29, 0.35, and 0.24, on subsurface flow were 0.43, 0.48, and − 0.41, and on surface sediment were − 0.21, −0.31, and 0.24, respectively. These results suggest the presence of a potential rainfall-intensity threshold, beyond which the regulatory effects of root–pore structure on runoff partitioning and sediment reduction become substantially weaker.

title: Analyzing the interaction mechanism between the loose rock aquifer system and river based on the Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes equations
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yudong Guo, Yuan Gao, Xiaonong Hu, Xiaoguang Wang
abstract: Understanding the interaction between rainfall-driven unconsolidated rock aquifer systems and riverbank processes, particularly the flow behavior and dynamic saturation processes of groundwater within various media of the unconsolidated rock aquifer during such interactions, holds significant theoretical guidance for the accurate assessment and sustainable development and utilization of such groundwater resources. Currently, the mechanisms governing this interaction remain unclear, and existing models struggle to characterize microscopic flow behavior, turbulence effects, and the dynamic evolution of medium saturation in macro-porous media. To address these issues, this study develops a three-dimensional gas–liquid two-phase flow model that couples the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method, Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations, and dual-continuum theory, and defines two dimensionless parameters-dynamic hydraulic tortuosity and characteristic time ratio—for quantitative analysis. The results show that rainfall intensity governs the shift in recharge-discharge direction between media and the distribution of runoff. Under high-intensity rainfall, rapid drainage through macropores raises river levels and induces river recharge to sedimentary layers, altering aquifer-river interaction behavior. The effects of turbulent eddy viscosity and inertial resistance modify hydrological response characteristics. Compared to laminar flow assumptions and the Boussinesq semi-analytical solution based on homogeneous Darcy flow, the RANS numerical solution exhibits lower drainage peaks, peak lag, and multi-peak fluctuations, reflecting the dynamic storage and buffering capacity of the aquifer system. Dynamic hydraulic tortuosity decays exponentially with increasing rainfall, representing the physical process in which the characteristic length of groundwater motion is progressively reduced by the constraints of the medium skeleton. The characteristic time ratio of macropore flow to matrix flow transitions from a power-law increase to an exponential jump, indicating a shift in system dominance from matrix flow to macropore flow on the temporal scale. This study provides a microdynamic basis for the accurate assessment of unconsolidated rock groundwater resources and the prevention and control of flood disasters.

title: Refining image-based approaches for river monitoring: a focus on graphical enhancement and software parameter sensitivity
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Francesco Alongi, Robert Ljubičić, Silvano Fortunato Dal Sasso, Leonardo Valerio Noto
abstract: Image-based techniques for estimating river surface velocity include traditional Large-Scale Particle Image Velocimetry (LSPIV), which infers tracer displacement by computing cross-correlation between pairs of consecutive frames, and optical flow approaches, which derive motion from image intensity gradients. Their accuracy strongly depends on image quality and processing configurations. However, the influence of enhancement techniques and parameter settings on large-scale velocimetry has not yet been systematically explored, due to complex interactions between field conditions, enhancement methods, and software-specific options. As a result, most studies still rely on authors’ experience and the processing tools available in the selected software. This study presents a sensitivity analysis evaluating the impact of different combinations of graphical enhancement filters and software parameterizations under varying environmental conditions. Image-based measurements were performed in two case studies in Sicily (Italy): the Oreto and Platani rivers. Acquired videos were pre-processed applying enhancement filters and multiple parameter configurations were tested. Analyses were performed using PIVlab and SSIMS-Flow, each tested with distinct processing setups. Overall, 1296 surface velocity fields were derived and compared to ADCP reference data. Water clarity and background complexity were objectively quantified using the Normalized Difference Turbidity Index (NDTI). Results demonstrate that both filter selection and software settings significantly influence image velocimetry accuracy. PIVlab, relying on cross-correlation, showed greater robustness in visually complex scenarios, while SSIMS-Flow, based on intensity gradients, achieved higher accuracy in uniform and turbid conditions. Poor performance generally corresponded to unsuitable filter-parameter combinations. Overall, the proposed framework helps refine image-based velocimetry workflows for more accurate field implementations.

title: Geodetic evidence of water mass loss from global navigation satellite system measured land uplift in Türkiye
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Kutubuddin Ansari, Emine Tanır Kayıkçı
abstract: This study quantifies terrestrial water storage (TWS) variations in Türkiye (2009–2024) using vertical land motion derived from a dense Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) network. Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) was applied to separate long-term deformation from seasonal oscillations in GNSS height time series, and elastic loading inversion was performed to convert vertical displacement into monthly equivalent water height (EWH) estimates. The resulting monthly GNSS-based TWS estimates were validated with Global Land Water Storage (GLWS), Global Land Data Assimilation (GLDAS)-Noah and Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) products. Results reveal pronounced TWS depletion-induced uplift across Southeastern Türkiye and Central Anatolia, reflecting groundwater stress in agricultural basins, while coastal and northern regions show positive water anomalies controlled by precipitation and snowmelt recharge. Seasonal amplitudes peak over the Black Sea and western regions, with phase shifts showing earlier TWS maxima in eastern snow-fed basins. Although GNSS-derived amplitudes are lower due to the sparse network and inversion smoothing, strong seasonal coherence with GRACE, GLDAS, and GLWS confirms the robustness of the approach. Overall, this work provides the first GNSS-based hydro-geodetic assessment of TWS over Türkiye and demonstrates GNSS as a complementary tool for drought monitoring and climate-driven water-storage evaluation.

title: A physics-guided and interpretable machine learning framework for rapid flood inundation mapping in complex flood retention areas
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Changjun Zhu, Ting Zhang, Qiang Ma, Aiqing Kang, Yunpeng Bai, Chengjian Wang, Philippe Gourbesville
abstract: Rapid and accurate flood mapping using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery is a critical tool for emergency response. While machine learning (ML) models have significantly enhanced the accuracy and efficiency of flood mapping, their “black box” nature limits their trustworthiness for critical emergency response applications. To address this issue, we developed an interpretable flood mapping framework based on Gaofen-3 (GF-3) SAR imagery that fuses remote sensing physics with data-driven analysis. The framework comprises three core components: (1) a novel physics-guided feature, the Generalized Normalized Difference Polarization Index (GNDPI), which transforms skewed backscatter data into a more separable bimodal distribution; (2) a Random Forest (RF) classification model incorporating multi-source features, including Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM), Local Binary Pattern (LBP), and Haar Wavelet; and (3) the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method, utilized to interpret the model’s decisions. The framework was successfully applied to the Dongdian flood retention area (DFRA) during China’s “23·7″ major flood event, yielding high accuracy (Overall Accuracy (OA) = 97.72%, Kappa = 0.953). In model comparisons, the RF model demonstrated over four times the computational efficiency of XGBoost, with a minimal 0.11% loss in accuracy, proving its practical value for emergency scenarios. Crucially, SHAP analysis revealed that the model learned a physically consistent decision logic, prioritizing features for macroscopic smoothness and microscopic uniformity, and leveraging complex feature interactions to differentiate water from non-water pixels. This study’s framework not only improves flood mapping performance but also demystifies the model’s decision logic via SHAP, offering a transparent and robust tool for rapid emergency response in data-scarce basins.

title: N 2 O emissions and driving factors of coastal agricultural drainage ditches: implications for the nitrogen cycle
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Zhenqi Shi, Xiang Liu, Dongli She, Alimu Abulaiti, Junhan Zhao, Yihua Huang
abstract: Agricultural drainage ditches are important sources of nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions associated with non-point source pollution. In coastal agricultural ditches, shallow groundwater fluctuations and tidal intrusion cause persistent salinity variations, which may alter N2O production, emission fluxes, and emission efficiency. However, quantitative evidence linking salinity fluctuations to N2O emission patterns in coastal agro-ecosystems remains limited. In this study, a two-year field survey was conducted in coastal agricultural drainage ditch systems in Jiangsu Province, China, from 2023 to 2025. Physicochemical properties, dissolved N2O concentrations, indirect N2O fluxes, and N2O emission factors (EF5) were monitored across ditch networks with increasing salinity from inland ditches to estuarine outlets. Key environmental drivers were identified using statistical analyses and random forest modeling. N2O emissions showed clear seasonal variation, with higher values in spring and summer and lower values in autumn and winter, consistent with periods of intensive agricultural activity. Spatially, main and branch ditches acted as N2O emission hotspots, whereas estuarine sites showed the lowest emission levels. The mean EF5 was 0.0009, lower than the updated reference values for rivers (EF5r = 0.0026) and groundwater/surface drainage (EF5g = 0.0060), while the mean indirect N2O flux was high at 440.29 μg N m− 2h− 1, indicating low emission efficiency but strong emission intensity. Temperature, electrical conductivity (EC) and the DOC:DIN ratio were identified as key factors regulating N2O emissions. N2O emissions increased within the intermediate EC range observed in this study (391–1470 μS cm−1), but was suppressed when EC exceeded 1693 μS cm−1. These findings suggest that coastal agricultural drainage ditches may contribute substantially to regional greenhouse gas budgets despite low EF5 values, and that DOC:DIN can serve as a robust predictor for refining N2O emission-factor estimates across salinity gradients.

title: An integrated framework for identifying throughfall spatiotemporal patterns: revealing dry zones as potential markers of pattern persistence
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Feng Xiong, Chuan Yuan, Yafeng Zhang, Yanting Hu, Zhiyun Jiang, Kazuki Nanko, Qin Liu, Sheng Wang, Yaoyan Li, Delphis F. Levia
abstract: Throughfall temporal stability is critical for maintaining spatial consistency in soil water amount and nutrient inputs, serving as a fundamental pillar for the structural and functional stability of vegetated ecosystems. However, traditional time stability plots rely on subjective visual interpretation. Quantitative alternatives like the relative difference and Spearman rank correlation coefficient methods fail to differentiate the specific contributions of distinct throughfall regimes (dry vs. wet zones) to overall stability. This study developed an integrated framework coupling Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) with geostatistical analysis and statistical metrics, including the coefficient of variation in ranks (CVr) and global Moran’s I. Validated using field data from two dominant shrubs (Caragana korshinskii Kom. and Salix psammophila C. Wang & C. Y. Yang) in the semi-arid Loess Plateau of China, this framework accurately quantified species-specific throughfall spatiotemporal patterns: S. psammophila exhibited greater spatial heterogeneity and temporal stability along direction and distance gradients. Spatial autocorrelation examination via Moran’s I confirmed significant clustering in throughfall distribution (p < 0.05). GMM-identified dry zones, receiving significantly less throughfall (65.0% vs. 77.1%, p < 0.001), maintained higher stability evidenced by smaller CVr (23.4% vs. 68.5%, p < 0.01). They functioned as potential markers for the persistence of overall throughfall patterns, distinct from wet zones acting as biogeochemical hotspots. Therefore, this framework provides a mechanistic tool to decipher throughfall spatiotemporal pattern, enhancing the predictability of throughfall fluxes and offering new insights into ecosystem stability particularly in water-limited environments.

title: Process-informed feature engineering for explainable optimization-driven AI in groundwater-level prediction
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Isa Ebtehaj, Amani Aissi, Afshin Amiri, Hossein Bonakdari, Silvio José Gumiere
abstract: Accurate prediction of groundwater levels is crucial for sustainable water management, yet most machine-learning approaches remain black boxes that overlook delayed recharge and cumulative hydroclimatic effects. To address this gap, this study developed an explainable, optimization-driven artificial intelligence framework integrating Bayesian optimization with XGBoost to capture temporal dependencies and identify dominant hydroclimatic controls in the Bécancour River Basin, Québec, Canada. The framework combines automatic hyperparameter tuning with process-informed feature engineering, incorporating lagged discharge, temperature, precipitation, and rolling and antecedent indices representing cumulative hydrological effects. A 12-year daily hydro-meteorological dataset (2010–2022) was used to evaluate model performance across monitoring wells. The baseline BOXGBoost model captured overall groundwater dynamics but exhibited spatial inconsistencies in upland regions, whereas process-informed features produced consistent improvements across wells. Process-informed engineered features markedly improved performance, achieving mean Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and coefficient of determination (R2) values of ∼ 0.92 and a Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) of ∼ 0.90, and reduced Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) to ∼ 0.14 m and ∼ 0.10 m, respectively. Relative to the baseline model, the enhanced framework increased NSE and R2 by about 81%, improved KGE by 53%, and reduced RMSE and MAE by about 56%. To further assess robustness, a temporally ordered validation (train-on-past/test-on-future) was conducted, confirming that the model maintains strong predictive performance under realistic forecasting conditions with only a limited impact on performance. SHAP-based analysis revealed that lagged features alone account for 46.46% of the total contribution, followed by rolling statistics at 23.30%, with water temperature (17.8%) and discharge at key stations (10.5% and 9.9%) among the most influential individual predictors. Together, lag and rolling features account for nearly 70% of the predictive importance, confirming the dominance of delayed recharge and cumulative hydrological responses. The BOXGBoost framework delivers accurate and interpretable groundwater-level predictions and supports groundwater monitoring, drought forecasting, and sustainable water management under variable hydroclimatic conditions.

title: Multicomponent geochemical reactions control arsenic mobilization in groundwater: novel insights from machine learning and geochemical model
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part A Author(s): Yanbo Feng, Shaogang Dong, Qingqiu Hou
abstract: Redox sensitive elements, including carbon (C), nitrogen (N), sulfur (S), iron (Fe), and manganese (Mn), play critical roles in groundwater arsenic (As) cycling. However, the behavior of As under the simultaneous influence of multiple interacting geochemical cycles remains poorly understood. In this study, self-organizing maps (SOM) and absolute principal component scores-multiple linear regression (APCS-MLR) were applied to identify the dominant mechanisms controlling As mobilization and transformation in groundwater. Based on these analyses, a multicomponent inverse geochemical model (MC-IGM) was developed for the Hasuhai Basin, China to elucidate coupled C-N-S-Fe-Mn-As cycling in groundwater. Integrated PCA-APCS-SOM analysis further identified four dominant factors controlling geogenic As contamination in groundwater, including geogenic sources (30.75%), Fe/Mn oxide redox transformations and anthropogenic inputs (35.63%), evaporative processes (0.97%), and water–rock interactions (32.66%). Geochemical modeling indicates that the redox cycles of Fe/Mn oxides govern the interconversion between As(III)/As(V). Heterotrophic dissimilatory NO3 − reduction to NH4 + (h-DNRA), organic nitrogen (Org-N) mineralization, sulfate reduction, and methanogenesis promote the enrichment of As. In contrast, nitrification enhanced As adsorption through coupling with Fe/Mn oxidation process. Collectively, these findings identify carbon cycling as the central process coupling N, S, Fe, and Mn transformations, ultimately controlling As mobility and speciation.

title: Monitoring the gravel packing process during completion of a geothermal well using distributed fiber optic sensing
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 140 Author(s): J. Hart, M.P. Lipus, C. Wollin, A. Saadat, C. Cunow, S. Kranz, T. Reinsch, C.M. Krawczyk
abstract: An efficient, safe, and sustainable geothermal energy supply depends on reliable well completion and monitoring technologies. Gravel packing is a process in well construction where the space between the filter screen and the formation is filled with gravel. This process can be crucial for producing sand-free fluid with minimal head loss. However, conventional wireline monitoring methods, such as manual bathometers or density logs, provide only discrete or post-placement information, leaving real-time downhole processes unobserved. This lack of continuous feedback creates operational uncertainties and leads to suboptimal decisions that can threaten well construction and reduce the well's efficiency. Here, the gravel packing of a 450-meter-deep exploration well designed for High-Temperature Aquifer Thermal Energy Storage (HT-ATES) in Berlin, Germany, was investigated using a fiber-optic sensing cable attached to the production casing. The study first evaluates the feasibility of simultaneous Distributed Temperature Sensing (DTS) and Distributed Dynamic Strain Sensing (DDSS, also known as Distributed Acoustic Sensing, DAS) for real-time gravel pack monitoring. Building on this, a combined interpretation of temperature cooling fronts, pump-induced wavefield reflections, vibrational energy anomalies, and low-frequency strain transients is used to identify the thermal and acoustic signatures of operational downhole processes such as fluid circulation and gravel pack placement, as well as of operational hazards such as caving, gravel bridging and collapse, screen clogging, and artesian fluid inflow. In situ observation of these theoretical concepts demonstrates the value of continuous fiber-optic measurements for improved understanding of downhole processes during well completion. The lightweight processing required to retrieve these data products makes the workflow suitable for edge deployment, enabling timely feedback to support proactive interventions that minimize operational risks and enhance well efficiency.

title: Substrate-specific bacterial and fungal communities in the Jukskei River plastisphere revealed by full-length amplicon sequencing
description: Publication date: 1 August 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1042 Author(s): Aubrey Dickson Chigwada, Chimdi Mang Kalu, Memory Tekere
abstract: The escalating crisis of plastic pollution in aquatic ecosystems has created a novel ecological niche known as the plastisphere, where microbial communities colonize plastic surfaces, influencing biogeochemical cycles, pollutant degradation, and ecosystem health. Despite global plastisphere research, studies in subtropical, eutrophic African urban rivers remain scarce, limiting insights into substrate-specific microbial assembly and bioremediation potential in polluted freshwater systems. Plastic debris in the Jukskei River, an urban waterway in Johannesburg, South Africa, hosts distinct bacterial and fungal communities on polyethylene (PE) and polystyrene (PS) surfaces. Attenuated total reflectance Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy revealed oxidative weathering (carbonyl indices 0.08–0.28) consistent with environmental aging. Targeted amplicon sequencing (full-length 16S rRNA and ITS regions via PacBio HiFi) demonstrated substrate-specific community composition (PERMANOVA, pseudo-F{1,8} = 3.45, R2 = 0.40, p < 0.01), with PE supporting higher genus-level evenness and taxa such as Romboutsia, Cutibacterium, and Sphingomonas, while PS was characterized by greater representation of Lactococcus, Clostridium sensu stricto, and lactic acid bacteria. Low-abundance potential pathogens at the genus level (Escherichia-Shigella, Streptococcus) showed statistically significant correlations with eutrophication indicators (BOD₅, nitrate) and cadmium, although no causal mechanisms were established. Additionally, the amplicon-based approach used was unable to confirm both species-level resolution and virulence potential. PICRUSt2 and FUNGuild predictions indicated the presence of broadly distributed metabolic pathways and guilds, but these inferences do not constitute evidence of active plastic biodegradation or specialized ecological roles. This study provides the first amplicon-based characterization of the plastisphere in a polluted African urban river, revealing substrate-driven bacterial assembly patterns and highlighting the need for future functional validation to assess bioremediation potential and public health risks.

title: A scalable Earth observation-based machine learning framework for high-resolution mapping and uncertainty assessment of climate-sensitive child health vulnerability in Bangladesh
description: Publication date: 1 August 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1042 Author(s): Md Moniruzzaman
abstract: Bangladesh remains highly vulnerable to climate-induced hazards that disproportionately affect child health, yet spatially explicit assessments of these risks remain limited. This study develops a scalable Earth observation–driven machine learning framework to map climate-sensitive child health vulnerability across Bangladesh at 1-km spatial resolution. Anthropometric and health indicators from the 2022 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) were integrated with multi-sensor satellite-derived environmental variables to generate high-resolution vulnerability surfaces and quantify prediction uncertainty. Georeferenced data from 674 DHS clusters (n = 8784 children) were combined with environmental covariates, including Land Surface Temperature (MODIS), precipitation (CHIRPS), vegetation indices (NDVI and EVI), and population density. Three supervised learning algorithms-Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine, and XGBoost-were trained using 80% of the dataset, with hyperparameters optimized through 5-fold cross-validation. The ensemble framework achieved the strongest predictive performance (R 2 = 0.683; RMSE = 7.65), outperforming individual models by 3.8%. Thermal stress, rainfall variability, and ecological productivity emerged as the dominant environmental determinants of vulnerability, collectively explaining 62% of model variance. The resulting maps revealed pronounced spatial disparities, with Rangpur exhibiting the highest vulnerability levels (67.3), while comparatively lower scores were observed in parts of Barishal and Sylhet (39.1). Bootstrap-based uncertainty analysis using 1000 iterations produced a mean uncertainty index of 4.8 ± 1.2, with elevated uncertainty concentrated in topographically complex regions. Hotspot analysis identified vulnerable clusters encompassing approximately 6.3 million children under five. The proposed framework provides a transferable approach for precision-oriented climate-health surveillance in data-constrained regions.

title: Machine learning-based prediction of antibiotic resistance gene distribution in agricultural soils under different climate change scenarios
description: Publication date: 1 August 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1042 Author(s): Meriem Kenzi, Meriem Benbernou, Hadjer Khelifa, Hadja Fatima Tbahriti
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in agricultural soils represent a major public health concern, as climate change is believed to augment their dissemination and abundance. Understanding the impact of future climate change scenarios on ARG abundance is essential to implement predictive and proactive One Health strategies. In this study, a total of 2301 soil samples from 67 countries across six continents were compiled from three global metagenome databases, namely NCBI SRA, MG-RAST, and JGI IMG/M. Six machine learning models, namely LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, Deep Neural Networks, and Logistic Regression, were used to predict ARG distribution patterns in agricultural soils, and their performance was evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation with metrics such as AUC-ROC, precision, recall, F1 score, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient. WorldClim 2.1 and CMIP6 models were used to project ARG distribution under three Representative Concentration Pathway scenarios, namely RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, and RCP 8.5, for the years 2050 and 2070. The LightGBM model achieved the best predictive performance, with an AUC-ROC of 0.957 (95% CI: 0.951–0.963), substantially higher than that of the other models, while the Deep Neural Networks model achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.891. The LightGBM model demonstrated high stability across cross-validation folds, with minimal fold-to-fold variance, defined as the standard deviation of AUC-ROC scores across the 10 folds (SD = 0.008). SHAP feature importance analysis identified soil temperature, pH, and organic carbon content as the top three factors influencing ARG relative abundance, with SHAP values of 0.342, 0.287, and 0.251, respectively. Annual precipitation and soil moisture level were also identified as significant contributors to ARG distribution. SHAP dependency plots revealed critical thresholds for ARG relative abundance, with a sharp increase observed independently when soil temperature exceeds 18 °C and when soil pH drops below 6.5. Furthermore, a non-linear accelerating increase in ARG abundance risk was observed as climate change intensity worsened across scenarios. Projections for future climate change scenarios indicate a potential 34.7% increase in high-risk ARG zones by the year 2070, with the largest changes expected in South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Mediterranean regions. Paired t-tests revealed significant differences in performance among all models (p < 0.001). These findings demonstrate that gradient-boosting methods such as LightGBM outperform deep learning approaches for ARG prediction from soil microbiome data, offering higher accuracy and interpretability. As climate change is projected to increase ARG risks in a non-linear manner, the development of climate-adaptive agricultural practices and global surveillance systems is urgent. This framework provides actionable risk-mapping tools to support precision farming and region-specific policy interventions within the One Health approach.

title: GeoAI for polar vegetation mapping and hydrological interactions: A systematic review
description: Publication date: 1 August 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1042 Author(s): Narmilan Amarasingam, Mariapina Vomero, Arthur Platel, Cassandra Newman, Sharon A. Robinson, Barbara Bollard
abstract: Remote sensing (RS) and Artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly applied to monitor vegetation and hydrology in the Arctic and Antarctic, where logistical and environmental constraints make fieldwork difficult. These technologies offer new opportunities to track ecological change, but the extent, consistency, and methodological quality of current applications have not been systematically reviewed. This study presents the first PRISMA 2020 based systematic synthesis of AI enhanced RS, collectively termed GeoAI, applied to Arctic and Antarctic environments (2005–2025; 116 studies). Publication activity has expanded significantly since 2018, driven by the convergence of uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV), multispectral imaging, satellite archives, and deep learning (DL). Bibliometric and conceptual-network analyses reveal a rapid shift from isolated ecological monitoring toward integrated, data-fusion frameworks linking vegetation, hydrology, and climate processes. Classical machine learning approaches remain foundational, while DL-based convolutional neural-network architectures are emerging as powerful tools for fine-scale segmentation and prediction. Most studies still operate at the landscape scale, with few achieving full UAV-to-satellite integration, exposing persistent spatial-resolution and validation gaps. Vegetation hydrology coupling is reported in most cases, though subsurface and process-based monitoring remain limited. Spectral-index analysis reveals a persistent reliance on greenness metrics, yet there is a growing shift toward pigment, moisture, and cryptogam-sensitive indices that more accurately capture plant physiological function and microclimatic interactions. This review establishes the empirical foundation for next-generation polar monitoring, emphasising hierarchical UAV-to-satellite fusion, open benchmark datasets, and explainable, ecologically grounded AI as essential pathways for scalable, climate-adaptive conservation of Earth's fastest-changing regions.

title: Silent Spill - maritime microplastics from vessel coatings
description: Publication date: 1 August 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1042 Author(s): T. Maes, A.L. Lusher, K. Pazdro, A. Pouch, M. Mazurkiewicz, S. Hjelset, M. Folbert, K. Lagiewka
abstract: Paint-derived particles are increasingly recognised as a major contributor to marine microplastic pollution, yet emissions from active vessels under routine operational conditions remain poorly characterised. We tested the hypothesis that exposed deck coatings on operational ships continuously generate and accumulate paint-derived micro- and meso-particles in the absence of maintenance activities. Samples were collected from accumulation zones adjacent to drainage points on three vessel types: an offshore support vessel, a container ship, and a liquefied natural gas carrier. Size-fractionated material was analysed using microscopy, FTIR/NIR spectroscopy, and multispectral imaging. Across vessels, more than 90% of classified particles were paint-derived fragments or iron oxide-rich corrosion products, while a minor fraction consisted of synthetic polymer fibres and fragments. Although the study design does not allow calculation of emission rates per unit area, the consistent presence and dominance of coating-derived debris across vessel types provide field-based evidence that routine weathering of deck coatings represents an ongoing and currently unregulated source of micro-sized particulate pollution. These findings identify exposed ship superstructures as a previously undercharacterised emission pathway and support the inclusion of coating degradation in ship-borne microplastic inventories and maritime sustainability frameworks.

title: Soil microplastics as carriers of organic pollutants: Sorption mechanisms and environmental behavior
description: Publication date: 1 August 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1042 Author(s): Jinghao Peng, Binyan Cheng, Lin Jiang, Qian Du
abstract: Soil is a major aggregate of microplastics and organic pollutants (antibiotics, pesticides). The long-term coexistence of microplastics and these organic pollutants in soil leads to inevitable interactions, which in turn affect their environmental behaviors. Based on recent research findings on microplastics in agricultural and urban soils, it is found that agricultural soils receive a large amount of microplastic inputs mainly through plastic mulching films, sewage sludge, compost, and atmospheric deposition, while microplastics in urban soils mainly originate from traffic, landfills, and industrial activities. Besides, the inherent characteristics of microplastics (polymer type, particle size, crystallinity, surface chemical properties), the chemical characteristics of antibiotics and pesticides (ionization, hydrophobicity, functional groups), and key environmental parameters (pH, ionic strength, soil depth, mineral composition, and dissolved organic matter) all affect the adsorption behavior and mechanism of microplastics on organic pollutants. Aging, dissolved organic matter, clay minerals, and biofilms can significantly alter the surface of microplastics, transforming the adsorption mechanism from simple hydrophobic partitioning to a complex interplay involving hydrogen bonds, electrostatic attraction, and π-π interactions. These processes can change the mobility, bioavailability, and persistence of the combined pollutants, thereby having a continuous negative impact on soil organisms, terrestrial food webs, and potential groundwater pollution. Therefore, it is imperative to reduce emissions at the source and develop soil risk management strategies as soon as possible to mitigate the long-term threats these emerging compound pollutants pose to soil ecological functions and human health.
